title: Wastewater Treatment Operations and Process Control
audience: Experienced municipal wastewater operators and shift supervisors.
prerequisites: Working familiarity with a treatment train, laboratory reports and metric units. A calculator and access to the linked readings are required.
introduction: Work a fictional Millhaven shift from incoming load through biological treatment, clarification, nutrient control and solids handling. Build calculations and a defensible handover from imperfect evidence.
delivery: Self-paced online pilot: complete 6 modules on your own schedule with case exercises graded automatically, source reading, active-time tracking and a server-graded final assessment. A non-credit pilot learning record is issued automatically after all requirements are met. The seven-hour daily recording limit applies across courses. Breaks and idle periods are excluded. Planned duration requires a timed pilot; no approved CEUs are awarded.

modules.title: Process boundaries and incoming load
objectives: Draw a control boundary that identifies recycle streams.
Distinguish concentration, flow and daily mass loading.
modules.lesson:
### Follow the material, not just the pipe
A wastewater treatment train transfers and transforms material. Screening removes gross solids; biological treatment transfers part of the incoming organic material into biomass; clarification separates suspended material; sludge handling concentrates the captured solids. A clear effluent concentration alone does not describe the mass leaving a plant. Flow and concentration must represent the same period and sampling boundary.

For a daily load, **kg/day = m³/day × mg/L ÷ 1,000**. At 8,000 m³/day and 180 mg/L, the incoming load is 1,440 kg/day. If wet-weather flow doubles while concentration falls to 110 mg/L, load becomes 1,760 kg/day. Dilution has reduced concentration while increasing mass. Neither concentration nor daily mass describes every short-duration peak.

Draw the measurement boundary before adding streams. A headworks flow meter upstream of a sidestream return does not measure that return. A downstream meter may already include it. Adding the same return twice creates a fictitious load. Similarly, an internal return-activated-sludge flow circulates material; it is not an external solids loss when calculating whole-system solids retention time.

Process decisions also have authority boundaries. An operator can identify a risk and make an authorized response; the exercise does not authorize bypassing treatment, entering confined spaces, defeating interlocks or changing approval conditions. Record the responsible role and controlling facility procedure. Use the Ontario operator guide for role context and the EPA primer for treatment concepts, keeping jurisdiction separate.

modules.title: Build a trustworthy process dataset
objectives: Calculate removal and identify uncertainty in a comparison.
modules.lesson:
### A precise calculation can answer the wrong question
A laboratory result has an identity: location, collection time, sample type, method, result basis and any qualification. The apparent precision of a number does not remove these attributes. A morning grab and a 24-hour composite do not necessarily describe the same wastewater. A downstream result may reflect a different parcel because of hydraulic travel and mixing.

For comparable daily boundaries, estimated removal is (incoming mass − outgoing mass) ÷ incoming mass × 100. With 1,500 kg/day entering and 75 kg/day leaving, estimated removal is 95%. If incoming and outgoing flows differ, use each flow separately. An unqualified concentration-only percentage assumes equal flows and representative matching periods.

Below a reporting limit is not zero. A result of less than 2 mg/L at 10,000 m³/day supports an outgoing load below 20 kg/day under the stated sampling assumptions; substituting zero would overstate certainty. Likewise, a field probe marked overdue is neither automatically false nor automatically usable for every decision. Seek a documented independent check and retain the original result with its qualification.

Build a data-quality table before diagnosing the process. Mark each value as usable for the intended comparison, provisional or unsuitable, and say why. That decision is specific to the question: an instantaneous alarm may justify urgent verification even though it cannot establish the daily average.

modules.title: Biomass, oxygen and clarification
objectives: Separate hydraulic, biological and settling evidence.
Calculate SVI and distinguish an observation from a diagnosis.
modules.lesson:
### One symptom can have several causes
An increasing secondary sludge blanket may reflect a solids inventory problem, poor settling, changing hydraulic load or a return-sludge equipment problem. Increasing the return flow is not a universal remedy: it changes clarifier hydraulics and redistribution of solids and must be evaluated within the facility's operating envelope.

The sludge volume index is **SVI (mL/g) = 30-minute settled volume (mL/L) × 1,000 ÷ MLSS (mg/L)**. At a settled volume of 300 mL/L and MLSS of 3,000 mg/L, SVI is 100 mL/g. A changed index is evidence about the standardized settling test, not proof of a particular organism or a universal pass/fail limit. Record test procedure, sample mixing, timing and concentration. Diluted tests must be identified and cannot be compared casually with undiluted results.

Dissolved oxygen is local and time dependent. A reading at one basin end does not establish conditions throughout the basin. A falling value, increased ammonia and a rising load are consistent with oxygen limitation, but probe performance, temperature, solids age, inhibition and sampling delays remain alternative explanations. Some responses require immediate authorized attention while slower laboratory evidence is collected.

Use an evidence ladder: observation, plausible mechanisms, discriminating checks, authorized action, verification. A mechanism becomes more credible when a predicted independent observation is found. Avoid making several large changes together: the resulting response may not identify which change mattered.

modules.assignment: Calculate both SVI values. rubric: Considers hydraulic load, settling and RAS delivery separately.

modules.facilitatorGuide: SVI is 100 then 150 mL/g. Both hydraulic and solids-return changes could contribute; standardized test deterioration adds a settling concern. Reject automatic pump-speed commands or a definitive filamentous-bulking diagnosis unsupported by microscopy and broader evidence. Require measurable follow-up, such as verified RAS delivery and blanket trend under comparable flow.

modules.title: Solids inventory, SRT and F/M
objectives: Calculate inventory and solids losses on a stated boundary.
Distinguish solids age from hydraulic residence time.
modules.lesson:
### State the mass basis before dividing
Solids retention time (SRT) is an inventory divided by a daily solids loss on a consistent boundary. It is not the hydraulic retention time. For this exercise, the defined inventory includes only aeration MLSS; clarifier inventory is explicitly omitted. That simplification must remain visible in the result.

A 2,000 m³ basin at 3,000 mg/L contains 6,000 kg MLSS. If waste sludge removes 400 kg/day and effluent removes 100 kg/day, the simplified SRT is 6,000 / 500 = 12 days. Ignoring the effluent loss would give 15 days and overstate this calculated age. RAS circulates inside the boundary and is not an additional external loss.

Food-to-microorganism ratio uses a stated organic loading basis and a biomass basis. Here **F/M = incoming BOD kg/day ÷ aeration MLVSS kg**. If BOD load is 1,200 kg/day and MLVSS inventory is 4,000 kg, F/M is 0.30 kg BOD/(kg MLVSS·day). Substituting MLSS changes the denominator and the meaning. Do not compare ratios from different conventions without reconciling them.

An estimated SRT describes the selected inventory and losses; it is not a direct instruction to set wasting. The current process condition, temperature, desired treatment, actual solids distribution and authorized operating plan determine how it should be interpreted. A measured high effluent solids loss can reduce retention even when the waste pump setting has not changed.
modules.evidence:
**M8 — daily solids worksheet**

Aeration volume 2,500 m³; MLSS 3,200 mg/L; MLVSS 2,400 mg/L. Waste flow 60 m³/day at 8,000 mg/L TSS. Effluent flow 10,000 m³/day at 12 mg/L TSS. Influent flow 10,000 m³/day at BOD 180 mg/L. RAS is 5,000 m³/day at 8,000 mg/L; it stays inside the selected system boundary.

M9: Clarifier solids inventory is unavailable. A sensitivity case doubles effluent TSS to 24 mg/L while holding other inputs fixed. All values are training averages, not approved targets.
modules.assignment: Submit a calculation sheet with MLSS inventory, MLVSS inventory, waste and effluent losses, simplified SRT and F/M. Recalculate SRT for M9. Explain the effect of excluding clarifier inventory and of incorrectly counting RAS as a loss. End with a 200-word request for the additional data needed before changing wasting.
rubric: Correct inventory and loss units and consistent bases.
Sensitivity calculation includes effluent solids loss.
Clearly labels the simplified SRT boundary and avoids prescribing a universal target.
modules.facilitatorGuide: Inventory 8,000 kg MLSS and 6,000 kg MLVSS. Waste 480 kg/day, effluent 120, total 600: SRT 13.333 days. BOD 1,800 kg/day: F/M0.30. At 24 mg/L effluent loss 240 and SRT 8,000/720=11.111 days. Adding omitted clarifier inventory to this same boundary would increase calculated SRT if losses stay fixed. RAS40,000 kg/day is internal recycling, not an external loss. modules.title: Nutrients, sidestreams and final treatment
objectives: Identify cross-process consequences of an adjustment.
modules.lesson:
### A small stream can carry a large load
A centrate or filtrate flow may be a small fraction of plant flow but carry concentrated ammonia or solids. Its effect depends on both mass and timing. For example, 100 m³/day at 500 mg/L ammonia-N contributes 50 kg N/day. If the return is delivered in four hours, its average return-period load is 12.5 kg N/hour, not the 2.08 kg/hour suggested by spreading it across a full day.

Nitrification transforms ammonia to oxidized nitrogen; denitrification removes oxidized nitrogen through a different biological pathway. A decline in ammonia does not by itself prove total nitrogen removal. Review ammonia, nitrate/nitrite and the relevant nitrogen basis together. Oxygen conditions, alkalinity, temperature, available carbon and biomass retention interact; none should be inferred from a single daily number.

Chemical phosphorus treatment transfers phosphorus to solids that must then be separated and handled. A lower soluble phosphorus result can coexist with a higher particulate load if solids escape clarification or filtration. Compare dissolved and total measurements on compatible samples before declaring the final effluent improved.

Write a change-impact map before modifying a return schedule or chemical dose. List the intended benefit, load redistribution, monitoring needs, equipment and storage constraints, authorization and stopping conditions. This is a decision-support exercise, not a chemical-handling or equipment-isolation instruction.

Centrate: 160 m³/day at ammonia-N 600 mg/L. Currently returned over 4 hours; proposal spreads the same daily volume over 12 hours. Main influent: 10,000 m³/day at ammonia-N 25 mg/L.

M11: Final effluent paired sample before a chemical trial: soluble P0.30, total P0.50 mg/L, TSS 6 mg/L. After trial: soluble P0.10, total P0.65 mg/L, TSS 18 mg/L. No flow change is recorded. These are two grabs, not a controlled trial.

modules.assignment: Calculate centrate and main influent nitrogen loads, the centrate share of their combined load, and return-period kg/hour before and after the proposal. Write a change-impact map and a separate interpretation of M11. Identify two missing facts that could block the proposed schedule and a monitoring plan that separates soluble removal from solids escape.
rubric: Correct daily and hourly load calculations.

Explains soluble versus total P without claiming causation from two grabs.
modules.facilitatorGuide: Centrate 96 kg/day, main 250, combined 346; centrate 27.75%. Return-period 24 kg/hour versus 8 kg/hour. Daily nitrogen load does not change. Capacity, pump range and operating authority must be checked. M11 suggests more particulate P (0.20 to 0.55 mg/L by difference) with higher TSS; it does not prove the chemical caused carryover. Ask for matched sampling, flow, clarifier/filter evidence and reproducibility. No credit for claiming 66.7% total-P improvement from soluble P alone.

modules.title: Integrated shift and defensible handover
objectives: Prioritize actions from conflicting process evidence.
Produce a handover with explicit owners and verification.
modules.lesson:
### Close the decision loop
A useful handover tells the next operator what is happening, what is known, what remains uncertain, what has been done, and what must happen next. A list of readings without interpretation transfers the analysis burden to the next shift. An overconfident diagnosis hides alternatives and can lock the next operator into a poor response.

Start with conditions that may require immediate response under the current facility procedure. Then distinguish checks that can quickly change the decision from slower investigations. Assign an owner and a time or event for each check. Record an action as completed only when there is evidence of execution; a request or a command is not completion.

Use calculations as bounded evidence. Daily averages may understate the incoming peak, an SRT estimate may omit clarifier inventory, and a result timestamp may follow the actual collection time by many hours. State the boundary alongside the number so another operator can reproduce it. Avoid changing several interacting controls without a monitored plan and the appropriate authority.

In a self-check, defend an alternative hypothesis and identify what observation would change your priority. Good process control is not stubbornness: it is a traceable response that can be revised when new evidence arrives. The final assessment checks the concepts; the practical is separately reviewed against every acceptance criterion.
modules.evidence:
**M13 — 07:00 handover packet**

Use M6–M12. At 07:10, maintenance verifies RAS actual flow 160 m³/h with an independent method; command remains 260. At 07:20, a checked portable probe at the basin-end sampling point reads 0.9 mg/L versus online 0.8. At 07:30, the lab reports yesterday's composite ammonia-N6 mg/L; yesterday's reference was 2 mg/L. Today's composite is not complete.

M14: OIC requests a written priority plan by 08:00. No approval to change return schedule or wasting has been issued. Maintenance has acknowledged the RAS work request; restoration is not yet documented.

M15: By 08:00, forward flow falls from 650 to 500 m³/h. Blanket depth remains 1.6 m. There is no later ammonia result.
modules.assignment: Prepare an 800–1,200-word operational case file: evidence timeline, calculation appendix using M8 and M10, ranked first-hour actions, two competing explanations, approval requests, stopping/escalation conditions and next-shift handover. Distinguish requests from completed actions. Update your interpretation for M15 without declaring the event closed. Discuss the case with the instructor, revise your submission and complete the final assessment and evaluation.
rubric: Uses the new verified RAS and DO evidence accurately.
Includes correct SRT, F/M and sidestream calculations with limits.
Assigns owners and verifiable next steps without unauthorized operating commands.
Does not equate falling flow with restored biological performance.
modules.facilitatorGuide: Accept a range of priorities if the learner explains the risk and follows the fictional authority boundary. Expected calculations: SRT 13.33 d simplified, F/M0.30, centrate 96 kgN/day and 24 kg/hour current return. RAS delivery discrepancy is now confirmed; maintenance completion is not. Portable DO supports the local reading but not every basin zone. Yesterday's ammonia cannot establish today's condition. M15 reduces one hydraulic stress but blanket and biological recovery remain unresolved. Return any case that declares compliance, approves bypassing, counts a maintenance request as repair, or omits the next owner. Allocate the last module assessment block to the final and evaluation as shown in the delivery plan.
